UPSTREAM: arch/x86: Utilize additional MTRRs in postcar_frame_add_mtrr In the current implementation of postcar_frame_add_mtrr, if provided size is bigger than the base address alignment, the alignment is considered as size and covered by the MTRRs ignoring the specified size. In this case the callee has to make sure that the provided size should be smaller or equal to the base address alignment boundary. To simplify this, utilize additonal MTRRs to cover the entire size specified. We reuse the code from cpu/x86/mtrr/mtrr.c. rockchip/rk3399: Move TTB to the end of SRAM We found that we may want to load some components of BL31 on the RK3399 into SRAM. As usual, these components may not overlap any coreboot regions still in use at that time, as is already statically checked by the check-ramstage-overlaps rule in Makefile.inc. On RK3399, the only such regions are TTB and STACK. This patch moves the TTB region back to the end of SRAM (right before STACK), so that a large contiguous region of SRAM before that remains usable for BL31. BRANCH=gru BUG=None TEST=Booted Kevin. Change-Id: I37c94f2460ef63aec4526caabe58f35ae851bab0 Signed-off-by: Julius Werner <jwerner@chromium.org> Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/384635 Reviewed-by: Simon Glass <sjg@google.com>

arm64: Take text_offset into account when searching for kernel location The ARM64 kernel needs to be relocated before boot to a location X+text_offset, where X must be 2MB-aligned and text_offset is provided by the kernel image (usually 0x80000). Since all memory below the kernel's location is unusable by the OS, finding the lowest location possbile is preferable. Our current search algorithm finds the next 2MB-aligned address after the start of a usable memory region, and then adds text_offset. This misses opportunities where the usable memory region starts after a 2MB boundary but early enough to fit once we add text_offset. This patch changes the search algorithm to take that into account. REDO: CHROMIUM: HACK: vop0 (big) pixel clock owns VPLL, nobody else uses There are a few possible problems with the 'normal' VOP clk tree: 1. At the whim of firmware, it's possible that VPLL will be initialized to something that is a multiple of our chosen pixel clock (266666 MHz). At the whim of common clock framework it's possible that VPLL will be chosen as the parent clock of the little VOP and be used by eDP. Now when we plug into type C then we'll want to change VPLL. Common clock framework is not currently smart enough to know that it should reparent the little VOP to CPLL / GPLL in this case. Instead the eDP pixel clock will be unexpectedly changed. Note that there are some "whims" there, but generally I don't like relying on un-guaranteed behavior. 2. Even if little vop gets cpll / gpll (YAY), the common clock framework could (on a whim) decide to also point the big VOP to cpll / gpll, maybe because you plug into a external display that happens to have pixel clock that can be made from cpll / gpll. Then you might change your display mode. Rather than reparent the big VOP back to vpll, the CCF might (on a whim) decide to change the rate of CPLL / GPLL, which would be a terrible idea. To summarize: the CCF has too much "automatic" behavior if you've got both CLK_SET_RATE_PARENT and you allow auto-remuxing (the default). It's going to bite us unless we do something to make sure that only the expected parents are used. Mark dummy for all the PLL which we don't want to assign to someone. That will give VPLL to big VOP. Little VOP will dynamically switch between CPLL and GPLL depending on the requested pixel clock. REDO: CHROMIUM: HACK: clk: rockchip: don't use frac clocks for VOP on rk3399 In order to get low jitter on the pixel clock, testing indicates that the fractional divider that can be a source to the VOPs needs to be _at least_ "divide by 20". Even with a source PLL of 2.4 GHz that gives us a maximum pixel clock of 120 MHz. This is not enough to support all pixel clocks that we expect to need. In theory we could be dynamic and use the fractional clock to make some of the stranger clock frequencies that are < 120 MHz. That would be ideal, but at the moment it's pretty hard because: 1. CLK_SET_RATE_PARENT doesn't work on fractional clocks. See http://crosreview.com/371641 2. We'd need to integrate the concept of jitter into the Rockchip clock framework and VOP client (maybe using clk_get_accuracy?) so we could set jitter requirements for the pixel clock and make sure that the fraction clock isn't configured in a way to give too much jitter. The above is a very difficult task. Until all that is done, let's simply hack out the connection to the fractional clock which will force common clock framework to just never use it.
